chapters.summary: Council staff welcomes attendees to the Parks and Recreation hearing, asks everyone to silence electronic devices, and states that no one may approach the dais. Staff then tells the chair the committee is ready to begin.
chapters.title: Council staff opens Parks Committee hearing and requests silence

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good afternoon and welcome to today's New York City Council hearing from the Committee of Parks and Recreation.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At this time, I'd like to remind everyone to please kindly silence your electronic devices and at no point is anyone to approach the dais.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chair, we are ready to begin.

chapters.summary: Chair Ty Hankerson identifies himself as chair of the Committee on Parks and Recreation and states the hearing will explore the state of water safety at city beaches and pools. He says the focus is how the city fared this past season with safety issues at Parks-operated beaches and pools.
chapters.title: Chair Hankerson opens hearing on water safety at city beaches and pools

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I'm Ty Hankerson, chair of the Council's Committee on Parks and Recreation.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Today's hearing will explore the state of water safety at the city's beaches and pools, specifically how the city fared this past season with safety issues at beaches and pools operated by the Parks Department.

chapters.summary: Hankerson says millions of people use city beaches and pools each year, and attendance has soared since the COVID pandemic. He questions whether the city has enough resources to meet public safety and recreational needs.
chapters.title: Hankerson highlights rising beach and pool use and resource questions

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Millions of people make use of the city's beaches and pools each year.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: In recent years have highlighted the extent of how crucial our parks, pools, and beaches are for New Yorkers like never before.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Since the COVID pandemic, attendance at pools and beaches have soared.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: But whether we have enough resources to sufficiently meet the public safety and recreational needs remains a huge question mark for our city.

chapters.summary: Hankerson says pools and beaches serve residents from all walks of life but have not reached full equitable potential. He calls drownings a leading cause of child death and a preventable crisis, with underserved communities facing the highest risk.
chapters.title: Hankerson frames water safety and drownings as preventable equity crisis

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: The city's pools and beaches represent some of the best examples of how municipal resources can be used to serve residents from all walks of life.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: But that doesn't mean these services have reached their full potential to adequately meet the needs of the entire city in an equitable way.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Water safety issues, specifically drownings, remain a big concern.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: It is sadly a leading cause of death for children, but it is a preventable crisis.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: can summon the will to divert enough resources to education on swimming and water safety.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: To highlight how much work we have to do, over 40 million adults in the United States do not know how to swim, with one in three African American adults being unable to swim.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Two in three African-American adults reporting to never have taken a swimming lesson, and three in four Hispanic adults reported to having never taken a swimming lesson.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Communities in our city that have historically been underserved educationally and economically have the highest risk of water-related injuries and death,

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: as these communities simply do not have easy access to pools, water safety instruction, and other types of water-based recreation, including my own district.

chapters.summary: Hankerson recounts that DPR historically assigned around 1,400 lifeguards by July 4 each season. A shortage reduced hires to 778 in 2022, 480 in 2023, and about 900 in 2024, and 2024 saw seven drowning deaths.
chapters.title: Hankerson recounts lifeguard shortage and 2024 drowning deaths

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: One obvious way to ensure that we improve water safety is to have enough lifeguards.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: DPR has historically assigned around 1,400 lifeguards to beaches and pools throughout the city by July 4th of each season.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: However, a lifeguard shortage hit the city hard during the 2022 beach and pool season.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: And DPR could only hire 778 lifeguards by that July.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: In 2023, there were only 480 lifeguards to start the season in May.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: In 2024, only about 900 were able to be hired.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: While some pools and beaches remained open, DPR had to adjust areas on beaches that could

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: remain open to swimming during the summer.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Unfortunately, 2024 was one of the most tragic seasons in recent memory, with seven drowning deaths.

chapters.summary: Hankerson notes DPR raised lifeguard pay and expanded recruitment and training. Lifeguard numbers rebounded to 1,082 in 2025 and 1,100 in 2026, but he says more work remains to bring staffing higher.
chapters.title: Hankerson notes lifeguard pay raises and staffing rebound

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: To its credit, DPR has recognized the problem and reacted by raising lifeguard pay rates and pursued numerous efforts to start the recruitment process earlier and adjust the training regimen to increase the number of potential applicants.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: The lifeguard numbers have thankfully rebounded with 1,082 lifeguard staffing pools and beaches in 2025.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: And 1,100 lifeguards this most recent season.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: However, it seems that there is still more work to be done to bring those numbers up even higher.

chapters.summary: Hankerson says lifeguards are critical but limited, so the hearing should take a holistic look at water safety. He lists expanding education, private partnerships, new pools, longer hours, surveillance, and water quality as key efforts.
chapters.title: Hankerson calls for holistic water safety approach and outlines bills

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: It's crucial that we recognize the work that lifeguards perform day in and day out, as they oftentimes are the primary reason why there aren't even

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: while there aren't even more emergencies at our beaches and pools.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: However, lifeguards can only do so much in ensuring our beaches and pools are as safe as possible.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: That's why I'd like to ensure this hearing takes a holistic look at examining what more we can do on this issue.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Some of these efforts include expanding water safety education and swimming lessons to more people, increasing engagement with private sector partners who have expertise in water safety, building more pools,

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: expanding operational hours to improve access, increasing surveillance efforts, and

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: and addressing larger environmental issues so that water quality is not harmful to swimmers and beachgoers.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thankfully, we will consider four pieces of legislation today that target some of these issues.

chapters.summary: Hankerson details four bills: Intro 1163 for digital rip current signs, Intro 262 to extend beach and outdoor pool season, Intro 957 for rip current signs at beach entrances, lifeguard chairs, and jetties, and Intro 1164 to map pools for nonprofit swim programming.
chapters.title: Hankerson details four water safety bills before committee

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Intro 1163, sponsored by myself, would require

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: the Department of Parks and Recreation to install digital signs at city beach entrances that would display visual and play audio announcements about the dangers of rip currents and other water safety hazards.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Intro 262, sponsored by Councilmember Krishnan, would extend the length of the beach and outdoor pool season to begin on the second Saturday in May and end on the second Sunday of each October, instead of the Sunday following Labor Day.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Intro 957, sponsored by Councilmember Brooks Powers, would require the Commissioner of DPR to post informational signs about riptides at each beach entrance, lifeguard chair, and jetty.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: And finally, Intro 1164, sponsored again by Councilmember Krishnan, would require DPR to identify swimming pools under the jurisdiction of city agencies.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: It would be feasible for nonprofit organizations that offer swimming and water safety programming to operate at such pools and include those pools on the interactive map operated by DPR.

chapters.summary: Hankerson thanks attendees and turns to Council Member Krishnan. Krishnan thanks the chair and Parks Department, says water safety and swimming are life-saving skills, and notes that children and teenagers drown on city beaches each summer.
chapters.title: Hankerson turns to Krishnan; Krishnan frames water safety as life and death

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I look forward to further discussing these issues today and welcome all who have come to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: And at this time, we're going to turn it over to the Department of Parks and Recreation.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Sorry, we're going to turn it over to my colleague, Councilmember Krishnan, for his statement.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Good to be back here, but nice to see you in the hot seat now and mean longer there.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But, you know, I've been so pleased to do the work together on our parks meeting to see your leadership.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And once again, on this issue as well, which is something that we all know.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I want to thank the Parks Department for joining us today for your testimony on this issue.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: It's an issue that with so many nonprofit organizations here, with the Parks Department, our council, I know we are laser focused on this issue.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And the reality is every year we see how.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Not only is it an issue of having access to water safely, to pools, like in my district that we don't have,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: but it's also every year that goes by, and we read the stories over the summer, of children, teenagers who have drowned on our city's beaches.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We know that water safety and addressing water safety is quite literally a matter of life and death, and that swimming itself, knowing how to be safe in the water, is a life-saving skill.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I know that all of us in city government are committed to solving this crisis together and doing all that we can.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I think every year that we revisit it and work on ways to increase the life card count, for example, find ways to expand access to swim programs is yet another step forward to get to a world where we do not have to see the news in the morning and read about

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: children suffering or dying because of our dangerous waters.

chapters.summary: Krishnan discusses his bill to expand pool and beach season as hot weather arrives earlier and lasts longer with climate change. He says the season should align with when New Yorkers actually use the water.
chapters.title: Krishnan advocates extending pool and beach season amid climate change

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: There's two pieces of legislation I wanted to just briefly touch on today that we are hearing that are mine.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: One is to expand pool and beach season in our city.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: As the hot weather stays longer, arrives earlier, and we know with climate change too, how important it is for New Yorkers to be able to have access to water as the temperatures heat up.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: For many, our beaches and pools are where New Yorkers and our families go to cool down on a hot day.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And one of the most important ways to make sure we can make our water safe is to actually expand permitted pool and beach season.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: That's a way to make sure when New Yorkers are getting in the water, because they will do that when the weather gets hotter, that we have the resources and staffing in place to make sure that...

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Pool and beach season lines up with the reality of when New Yorkers will use the water.

chapters.summary: Krishnan acknowledges the lifeguard shortage and progress made, but says more trained lifeguards and a creative pipeline are needed to extend the season. He says the cost of not acting is measured in lives, not just dollars.
chapters.title: Krishnan says longer season requires more lifeguards and pipeline

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: With that in mind, I do know that this is a difficult issue, and one of the issues is that we have to make sure we have enough lifeguards.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I know we have made progress on that issue since over my years as the chair of the Parks Committee up until today, but I know there's more work to be done as well, and I remain committed to working with you all, the Parks Department, everyone in this room,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: to solving that challenge together.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I know one goes lockstep with the other.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We need more lifeguards.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We need to create a pipeline of lifeguards, trained lifeguards.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We have to be creative about how we do so to make sure we can extend pool and beach season.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But I look forward to all of us working together to achieve that goal because

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: The reality is we have to.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: This is a necessity.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And no, the cost of not doing this is far too great of a cost to bear than simply dollars and cents.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: As we're talking about, it is lives at stake.

chapters.summary: Krishnan discusses his bill for Parks to partner with nonprofits on swim programs. He praises swim organizations filling gaps in districts without pool access and says he must leave but will review testimony.
chapters.title: Krishnan urges Parks partnerships with swim nonprofits

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: The other piece of legislation I have as well is about the Parks Department exploring the ways in which it can partner with nonprofits when it comes to swimming and swim programs.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I would also mention there as well and urge the Parks Department, as you all know, there is a phenomenal number of excellent swim organizations across the city that are really filling the holes where it comes to students, like in my own district, that don't have access to swim

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: and water safety classes otherwise.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And it would be great to find ways for the Parks Department to partner with and grow that collaboration between city government and swim organizations, many who are present today, too, to testify as well.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I look forward to a robust discussion on this piece of legislation as well and to the ways in which the Parks Department can work with nonprofits on the ground to expand

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: quite literally the pool of resources available to help children learn how to swim.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you all so much.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I unfortunately can't stay too long at this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: It's been quite a day, but I will make sure to review the testimony of both the Parks Department and the members of the public and nonprofit organizations who are here.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Hankerson reads a statement from Council Member Brooks Powers supporting Intro 957. The bill would require rip current safety signs at all bathing beaches in at least four languages with visual imagery.
chapters.title: Hankerson reads Brooks Powers statement on rip current signage

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I'm going to read the testimony, I'm sorry, the statement from Councilmember Brooks Powers regarding her bill.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Hangerston and members.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: of the Committee on Parks and Recreation for including Intro 957 in this critical hearing on water safety.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Intro 957 requires the Parks Department to post signs with safety information about rip currents at all bathing beaches under the department's jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: These signs will include information in at least four languages about the danger posed by rip currents and what to do if caught in one, as well as visual imagery.

chapters.summary: The Brooks Powers statement says Rockaway Beach saw 1.7 million visitors in 2024 and lifeguards responded to 73 emergencies there, over a third of city water emergencies. It cites over 100 U.S. rip current deaths annually and says rip currents account for over 80% of surf rescues.
chapters.title: Brooks Powers statement cites Rockaway Beach drownings and rip current rescues

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: In the Rockaways, the ocean is our front yard.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Our beachfront is a beloved summer destination, seeing 1.7 million visitors in 2024.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: But that beachfront also presents a recognized danger.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: And every summer, our community is too often brought together to mourn those we lose to drownings.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: In the most recent year, the Parks Department reported data.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Lifeguards responded to 73 emergencies on Rockaway Beach, more than a third of the 203 water emergencies in New York City pools and beaches over that period.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Our lifeguards are under a tremendous burden each summer to keep us safe, and informing beachgoers about the risk of rip currents is a common-sense preventative measure.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Across the city, we must do more to increase opportunities on our waterfront while mitigating the risk the ocean presents.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Intro 957 takes a meaningful step in preventing tragedies and water-based emergencies as rip current signage targets one of the greatest risks to beachgoers across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: A review of data reported

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: to the United States Life Saving Association found that there are over 100 deaths each year in the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Attributed to rip currents.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: It's accounted for over 80% of rescues performed by surf beach lifeguards.

chapters.summary: The statement thanks water safety advocates including the Water Safety Coalition, Rising Tide Effect, Swim Strong Foundation, LaRue Bay Area Collective, and Black Surfing Rockaway. It also thanks colleagues and the chair and looks forward to advancing Intro 957.
chapters.title: Brooks Powers thanks water safety advocates and surfing groups

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Residents of the Rockways and the millions of beachgoers across the city each year need this potentially life-saving information at every beach entrance, lifeguard, chair, and jetty.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you to the advocates who continue to fight for this legislation and for water safety across New York City, including the Water Safety Coalition, Rising Tide Effect, Swim Strong Foundation, and many others.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I also want to thank our local organizations advocating for increased surfing access, LaRue Bay Area Collective, and Black Surfing Rockaway, who are teaching young people in our community to enjoy our beaches safely.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you as well to my colleagues and the chair for their work on this issue.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I look forward to advancing this legislation, Council Members of Interbrooks Powers.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: All right.
