chapters.summary: Mark Focht identifies himself as First Deputy Commissioner and Chief Operating Officer for NYC Parks. He introduces Chief Bonnie Williams and Matt Drury and says they will update the committee on a successful and safe 2026 summer season.
chapters.title: Deputy Commissioner Mark Focht introduces Parks team and 2026 season

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Hankerson, members of the Park Committee and other members of Council.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: My name is Mark Folk.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: I'm the First Deputy Commissioner and Chief Operating Officer for New York City Parks.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Joining me today on my left is Chief Bonnie Williams, Chief of Special Programs, and on my right, Matt Drury, the Chief of Citywide Legislative Affairs.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: We are pleased to be here to offer an update regarding a very successful and safe 2026 summer beach and pool season.

chapters.summary: Focht says Parks is committed to aquatic recreation and safety. He reports the 2026 beach season was 114 days, 16 weeks, and the longest in a decade, with a record 16.7 million patrons visiting beaches and pools.
chapters.title: Focht reports record 16.7 million visitors and longest beach season in decade

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: NYC Parks has long been committed to improving New Yorkers'quality of life through aquatic recreation, promoting health, fitness, and safety awareness at both our beaches and pools.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Whether cooling off or getting fit, we know New Yorkers love to take a refreshing swim, and city beaches and pools are the primary getaway, summer getaway destinations for New Yorkers, many New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Due to the timing of Memorial Day and Labor Day this year, the summer 2026 beach season was the longest in a decade.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: It was 114 days, which is 16 weeks, which is four full.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: months and New Yorkers came out in droves and took advantage of that for four months.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: A record, and I will repeat, a record, 16.7 million patrons visited our beaches and pools this year and we're exceedingly proud that our guests enjoyed a fun,

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: family-friendly, clean and safe experience at both our beaches and pools.

chapters.summary: Focht says Parks certified 1,174 lifeguards this summer, the highest in four years and a nearly 50% increase since 2022. Lifeguards performed over 200 rescues, and there were zero fatalities or drownings while lifeguards were on duty.
chapters.title: Focht reports 1,174 lifeguards and zero on-duty drownings

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: It takes an incredibly hardworking team to make this a reality, including our maintenance and operations staff, aquatic staff, our Parks Enforcement Patrol colleagues, and most notably our lifeguards.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: We are pleased to report that we certified 1,174 lifeguards this summer, the highest staffing level in four years, and a close to 50% increase since 2022.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Our lifeguards rose to the occasion, performing over 200 rescues, and we are extraordinarily proud to report that there were zero,

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: zero fatalities or drownings while lifeguards were on duty at their chairs at all of our beaches and pools this past summer.

chapters.summary: Focht says Parks remains committed to returning to pre-pandemic staffing of roughly 1,400 lifeguards. Parks launched the 2026 recruitment campaign, with registration opening November 15 and the first qualifying test December 1, and training in all five boroughs.
chapters.title: Focht launches 2026 lifeguard recruitment campaign

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Looking ahead, though, as the councilman has mentioned, we remain committed to returning to our pre-pandemic levels of lifeguard staffing at roughly 1,400 lifeguards and are diligently working to achieve that goal.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: We have already launched the lifeguard recruitment campaign for the summer of 2026 with the

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Tagline, your strength, their safety, our team.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: And for everyone, I'm holding up a poster, which has been delivered to council members'offices, and we welcome you to help us distribute the information about our new lifeguard recruitment campaign.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: We are proud that this public awareness campaign produced entirely in-house by park staff.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Campaign materials are being distributed, and we, again, appreciate support from council members and all of our partners in the swim community to get the word out and help amplify our message.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: The registration portal actually opens this Sunday, November 15th, and the first qualifying test will be held on December 1st.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: So we're getting very close to beginning to qualify lifeguards for next summer already.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: With the help of agency partners, most noticeably NYC Public Schools, we will again qualify, train, and certify lifeguards in all five boroughs, so no candidates have to travel far from their home.

chapters.summary: Focht says Parks shares the Council's desire to expand access but Intro 262 presents budgetary, operational, and safety concerns. He says mid-May to mid-October would have 50-60 degree temperatures and minimal visitation, and seasonal workers would be unavailable.
chapters.title: Focht opposes Intro 262 season extension over budget and safety concerns

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Turning to the legislation being formally heard today, Introduction 262 would extend the operational season for beaches and outdoor pools and would increase the daily operating hours for beaches, outdoor pools, and indoor pools.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: We share the Council's desire to expand New Yorkers'access to swimming, but the legislation as drafted presents significant budgetary, operational, and safety concerns.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Beaches currently open for swimming on the Saturday of Memorial Day weekend and close

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: the Sunday after Labor Day.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Outdoor pool season is generally patterned on the school calendar, opening this after schools end in late June and closing again the Sunday after Labor Day.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: As currently drafted, the legislation would require that both beaches and outdoor pools open in mid-May and remain open until mid-October.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Times of the year when air and water temperatures are often range in the 50 to 60 degrees, leading us to expect that visitation would be exceedingly minimal.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Also, summer beach and pool operation entail hiring thousands of seasonal staff to serve as lifeguards, maintenance, and security personnel.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: The vast majority of our seasonal workforce consists of teachers, college students, and high school students,

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: all of whom would be unavailable during the proposed extensions as they are occupied, obviously, with their primary academic or professional pursuits.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: We are proud of our extensive staff recruitment efforts, but the stark reality is that employees required to maintain and safeguard our beaches and pools would simply not be available during the proposed extension.

chapters.summary: Focht says the bill's 8 p.m. closing would make it harder for lifeguards to see patrons. Swimming is currently prohibited after 6 p.m. at beaches and 7 p.m. at pools, and dusk in September and October occurs between 6:30 and 7:30.
chapters.title: Focht warns 8 p.m. closing would limit lifeguard visibility

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Additionally, the bill would require beaches and pools to remain open each day until 8 p.m.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Setting aside staffing challenges, lifeguards need to be able to see patrons in the water at either a beach or pool in order to safeguard them.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Their ability to do that becomes increasingly limited as does

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: dusk approaches.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: To safeguard patrons, swimming is currently prohibited after 6 p.m.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: At beaches and 7 p.m.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: At pools.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: With dusk occurring between 6.30 and 7.30 in September and October, lifeguards would not be able to see patrons in the water to respond to emergencies.

chapters.summary: Focht says current beach and pool hours are comparable to Long Island and New Jersey. He then introduces Intro 957 and Intro 1163, which would require rip current signage, and says Parks agrees patrons need to be informed.
chapters.title: Focht says current hours comparable to neighbors; addresses rip current signage bills

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: It is worth noting that the current operational hours and duration of our beach and pool season is comparable to other municipalities, including our neighbors

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: on Long Island and New Jersey, and offer New Yorkers the ability to stay cool when they need it the most.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Introduction 957 would require the installation of informational signage related to the dangers of rip current at every beach entrance, lifeguard chair and jetty under parks jurisdiction, and introduction 1163

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: would require the installation of digital signage at beach entrances regarding the danger of rip current.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Keeping our beachgoers safe is a top priority, and we agree that patrons need to be informed.

chapters.summary: Focht says only Rockaway Beach is classified as a true ocean beach with rip currents. Parks displays NOAA rip current posters in restrooms at all eight beaches, vinyl banners at Rockaway, multilingual signs at entrances and jetties, and signs on lifeguard chairs; lifeguards also visit schools.
chapters.title: Focht details existing rip current signage and school water safety visits

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Due to the geographic configuration of our beaches, only Rockaway Beach experiences rip currents, as it is classified as a true, it is our only beach classified as a true ocean beach.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: However, because of our strong dedication to swim safety, we display the official NOAA advisory posters about the danger of rip currents in public restrooms at all eight beaches.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: And I'm just holding up what one of these look like.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: It's the standard NOAA poster for rip current.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Again, posted at all public restrooms at all eight beaches.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: In addition, we post large vinyl banners with such dangers on the exterior restroom buildings at Rockaway.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: In accordance with New York State's and local health code requirements, we also display advisory signage in multiple languages at every beach entrance.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Which notes that patrons need to be aware of strong currents and sudden drop-offs, and safety signage is installed at each beach jetty or groin.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Additionally, we already display signs on the back of every lifeguard chair, reminding beach visitors that swimming is only permitted when lifeguards are on duty in their chairs.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: In recent years, we have arranged with NYC Parks Lifeguard to visit local public schools and teach students about water safety, focusing specifically on the danger of rip currents and the importance of swimming only when a lifeguard is on duty.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: As all of this illustrates, we are always open to exploring new avenues to better educate New Yorkers about the importance of swim safety.

chapters.summary: Focht says Parks is concerned the bills may cause public confusion. Digital signage would be expensive and hard to maintain due to sand, wind, salt spray, vandalism, and over 200 beach entrances; Intro 1164 would require Parks to assess non-Parks pools and map them, beyond its expertise and resources.
chapters.title: Focht raises concerns with digital signage and pool map bill

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: But we have concerns that these two bills, as currently drafted, may impose significant operational concerns and inadvertently lead to confusion for the public.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Specific to Introduction 1163, we believe that digital signage would be extremely challenging and expensive to maintain, to install and maintain in a beach environment.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Given the exposure to sand, wind, and salt spray, as well as the potential for vandalism.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: And I would like to note that across our eight beaches, we have over 200 individual entrances to our beaches.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Lastly, Introduction 1164 would require parks to consult with other city agencies that have jurisdiction over swimming pools regarding the feasibility of engaging with not-for-profit organizations

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: to offer swimming and water safety programming at such pools and to make related information available on an interactive map of swimming pools posted on our agency's website.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: We very much appreciate the Council's support for swim safety, and we are proud to offer free swim education and aquatic programs for thousands of New Yorkers every year,

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: provided by Parks employees working at our rec centers, our outdoor pools, and select NYC public school indoor pools.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: However, the agency does not have the expertise or resources to assess the appropriate use of city property that is not under our jurisdiction

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: or to advise when those facilities should be made available to non-city entities to provide additional programming.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Additionally, we believe that displaying information regarding non-park facilities on a map that is meant to relay information regarding park facilities would lead to unnecessarily public confusion.

chapters.summary: Focht says Parks shares the Council's water safety goal and is open to discussing alternatives. He closes with four numbers: 114 days, 1,174 lifeguards, 16.7 million patrons, and zero on-duty drownings, and looks forward to 2027.
chapters.title: Focht offers collaboration and closes with four season numbers

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Of course, we very much share the Council's goal of increasing awareness about the importance of water safety and would be happy to take further conversation with the Council and fellow city agencies to identify potential alternatives to achieve this important objective.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: We look forward to further discussion.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: discussing the legislation being heard here today and very much appreciate the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: I would, though, however, like to close by restating four numbers which define the successful and safe summer 2026 beach and pool season.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: It's a number of days in the beach season, 16 weeks, four months, the longest beach season in a decade.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: 1,174 certified lifeguards, the highest staffing since the pandemic, and a 50% increase in the last four years.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: 16.7 million is the number of patrons that we saw and hosted at our beaches and pools this summer.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Again, a record.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: And I would close with zero.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Zero being the number of drownings or fatalities while lifeguards were on duty in their chairs during the longest, hottest, and busiest beach season in over a decade.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: We look forward to building on this success and having an even greater beach and pool season in 2027.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Thank you for your continued advocacy and support for New York City Parks, and we would be happy to answer any questions you may have.

chapters.summary: Hankerson asks about lifeguard deployment and pay. Focht says Parks deployed 480 beach lifeguards and 680 pool lifeguards in 2026; starting pay is just below $23 per hour, escalates with experience, training is paid, and there is a $1,000 retention bonus under the collective bargaining agreement.
chapters.title: Hankerson asks Focht about beach vs pool lifeguards and pay

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: We're going to jump right in so that I can turn it over to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: And so I want to make sure there's enough time to hear from the public and advocates as well.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: So let's start here.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: What's the breakdown for lifeguards and beaches versus?

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: In the 2026 season, we deployed 480 beach lifeguards and about 680 pool lifeguards.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: 480 beach lifeguards and 680 pool lifeguards.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: What's the current starting pay for first-time lifeguards, and what is the pay scale for more experienced lifeguards, respectively?

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: So the starting salary is just below $23 an hour, which is competitive or higher than almost all of our peer beaches on New Jersey on Long Island.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: And then it escalates with years of experience.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: In addition, when you come into your training program and you successfully go through the 16-week training program, you are also paid for the time you spent training.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: And after your first year lifeguard, if you stay with us through Labor Day, you get a $1,000 retention bonus.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Would want to note that all of this is part of the collective bargaining agreement.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: So it's not simply on parks to be able to say we want to adjust the pay or it's all part of the collective bargaining agreement.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Do lifeguards at beaches receive the same pay as lifeguards at pools?

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Yes.

chapters.summary: Hankerson asks about DOE recruitment and qualifying tests. Williams says Parks works with NYC Public Schools in all five boroughs, distributes banners, works with PSAL, and sends digital toolkits; Parks hosted 49 qualifiers in 2026, starting December 1 and running through February.
chapters.title: Hankerson and Williams discuss DOE lifeguard recruitment and qualifiers

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Does DPR and DOE currently engage in any efforts to recruit and train students at DOE schools who may be interested in working as lifeguards?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Turn that over to Chief Williams.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember, for that question.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: Yes, we are engaged with New York City Public Schools.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: Currently, we are set up to do qualifiers for the upcoming season at New York City Public Schools in all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: We have distributed over 350 banners with our new marketing campaign that are going up at the schools, the high schools and intermediate schools.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: We also work very closely with the PSAL.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: We have our staff that go out and recruit at athletic events, swim meets.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: Football events, anything that the PSAL wants us to engage in.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: We also have an email blast that goes out with our digital toolkit to all parents and students in the New York City public school system.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Is this across all public high schools or select schools?

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: Yes, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: This is across all public high schools.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: We work very closely.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: We also sit on the Lifeguard Aquatic and Safety Task Force with many non-for-profits, YMCAs, and New York City public schools.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: So we get the information out, not only about the qualifiers, but just about swim safety.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: We've worked very closely with New York City Public Schools digital media team and our digital media team to get information about the qualifiers, recruitment, and water safety out on the social media.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: How many qualifying tests were hosted this year by Parks for Potential Lifeguards?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: And what were the test locations, the sites?

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: For the 2026 season, we hosted 49 qualifiers across all five boroughs in a combination of New York City parks, recreation centers, and New York City public school high schools.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: During what months are the qualifying tests held?

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: Last year, we started qualifiers in November, and we ran into February.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: This year, we are starting qualifiers December 1st and running until February.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: We wanted to give the swim teams a little more time to get up and get conditioning to get those kids ready to take the qualifier.

chapters.summary: Hankerson asks what standards must be met to qualify as a lifeguard. Williams explains sign-up, a free swim improvement program, a 16-week training program in all boroughs, skills and CPR training, written and practical exams, and an additional beach swim test for beach assignments.
chapters.title: Williams outlines lifeguard qualification and training process

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Can you provide a breakdown?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: of what standards need to be met to qualify to be a lifeguard during these tests?

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: Sure, that's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: So one, it starts with them signing up for a qualifier.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: In addition to signing up for the qualifier, if participants feel they need to get ready to take that,

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: our aquatics division also has the swim improvement program that's offered at different parks facilities that's available online they can register for.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: Once they take the qualifier and pass the qualifier, they can register for one of our 16-week training programs that we currently offer in all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: If they successfully pass and complete the training program, which consists of lifeguard skills, first aid, CPR skills, and pass the final written and practical exam, then they will be assigned to

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: a pool or beach facility.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: If they are assigned to a beach facility, when they get out to their beach, there is an additional swim test that they have to take because we want to make sure that they're beach ready.

chapters.summary: Hankerson asks about recruitment efforts and changes over the years. Williams describes marketing, over 700 mailings, digital toolkits to 500 stakeholders, job fairs, swim meets, and a task force; Focht adds that training and certification have expanded to all five boroughs, previously only Manhattan.
chapters.title: Williams and Focht detail expanded lifeguard recruitment efforts

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Can you describe the department's efforts to recruit lifeguards and what changes may have occurred over the years in the recruiting process?

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: That's a great question, and we're very excited to discuss the things that have happened, especially over the past three or four years.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: Number one, our marketing campaign every year, we've done over 60.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: 700 mailings, actual snail mail, and digital media toolkits that have been sent out to over 500 key stakeholders.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: We work closely with the elected officials, with the non-for-profits, with New York City public schools to get the word out about the marketing campaign and recruiting for lifeguards.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: Our team goes out to job fairs, swim meets, any event where we can get that word out that we are looking for lifeguards,

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: for them to sign up to get our email blasts on how to register for qualifiers.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: So that's one aspect.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: We also sit on the aquatic lifeguard and safety task force that I mentioned before with a lot of the not-for-profits around New York City.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: And we all work collectively, not only for parks, but for our constituents that are out there, how we can boost up those lifeguard numbers.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: So it's about communication.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: It's about having our lifeguards themselves actually go out and explain what an amazing job it is, how proud they are to be the lifeguards, and to show the young kids that are out there.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: Anyone can be a lifeguard as long as they put the work in and they can pass the qualifier in the training.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Councilmember, I would also add that we've mentioned it several times, but it is worth repeating that in the last several years, we expanded both the recruitment, the certification, and the training to all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: So that has not been the case in years past, even leading into the pandemic.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Training and certification happened in Manhattan, so people had to travel some distance.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: So we're very proud to offer it in all five boroughs.

chapters.summary: Hankerson acknowledges attending council members and asks about lifeguard turnover. Focht says Parks prefers retention rate, which was 79% this past year, with 865 lifeguards returning from 2025 to 2026, up from about 70%, due to salary, bonus, and work environment.
chapters.title: Hankerson acknowledges members and asks about lifeguard retention

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I neglected to do this.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I want to acknowledge that we have been joined by, I know he had to step out, Councilmember Krishnan, Councilmember Santososo, Councilmember Narcisse, Councilmember Marte, Councilmember Lee, Councilmember Morano.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: A couple more questions for me, and I'll turn it over to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: What's the typical turnover rate for lifeguards from year to year?

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member, for the question.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: We prefer to think of it as the retention rate, so the number of lifeguards that stay with us.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: And the retention rate this past year was 79%.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: So that's 865 lifeguards that worked for us in the summer of 2025, came back in the summer of 2026.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: That's almost a 10% increase in the last four years.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: We've traditionally been running about a 70% retention rate.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: We're now at 79%.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: So we like to think that's a reflection of many things, including the salary, the bonus, the work environment, many different things.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: But yes, it's a retention rate of 79%.

chapters.summary: Narcisse notes the zero on-duty drowning statistic but says young people still die in the water. She asks what recommendations Parks can offer; Focht says the core message is to swim only when a lifeguard is in the chair, amplified through digital ads on the MTA A train in the Rockaways.
chapters.title: Narcisse questions Focht on drownings outside lifeguard hours

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I'm going to turn it over to my colleagues, starting with Councilmember Narcisse.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I wish that the safety part, like zero, I see how you say zero, while the lifeguard was in the chair.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So having said that, while the lifeguard in the chair, there is zero.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But we still have...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Our young folks are dying in the water.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So to your knowledge, what kind of recommendation you can give us?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: At least we can do something about it because I want zero even after hours.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What can we do actually in your vision?

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Councilwoman, for the question.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: The message is the actions that can be taken is help to amplify our message, which is that you only swim when a lifeguard is in the chair.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: That is our constant message.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: It's everywhere.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: We're now doing it on digital ads with the MTA on the A train in Rockaways.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: So our message is constantly, whether you're at a beach or a pool, you only swim when a lifeguard is in the chair.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: That is the way to ensure that we're providing the oversight that's needed to keep the public safe.

chapters.summary: Narcisse suggests partnerships with high schools, junior highs, and colleges to reach young people. Williams says lifeguards visit schools for water safety assemblies focusing on rip currents and not swimming without a lifeguard, using drone videos; 70% of hired lifeguards were ages 16 to 18.
chapters.title: Narcisse urges school partnerships; Williams details water safety assemblies

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I love that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But another way I'm thinking is in high schools, in junior highs, in college, we can have that partnership.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: to make sure that they hear us loud and clear.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because most of our young folks are dying, usually from the high school age or early college that want to impress their children.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I mean, their friends, you know, that I think that can be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: If I may, I'd like to have the chief address that we've had great programming in high schools, and it's really great to see the young people interact with the lifeguards, many of whom are their peers.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Because, again, 70% of the lifeguards we hired this past year were ages 16 to 18.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: But Chief Williams.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: So in the past three years, our lifeguards themselves have gone out to high schools and intermediate schools in the five boroughs and have done water safety

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: assemblies, especially focusing on rip currents and not swimming when a lifeguard's on our duty.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: This is something that with the, I've stated before, we're part of the Aquatic Lifeguard and Safety Task Force.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: Other groups are doing this as well because we know how important it is to get that word out, especially to that targeted group of teenagers that

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: are going to go there when the beaches are not open.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: So our lifeguards, who is one of the most diverse group, they can identify with a lot of those kids that are out there.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: Those kids can see themselves in the lifeguards, and they're getting that message out about how important and critical it is to only swim when a lifeguard is on duty.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: With the drone videos that we show during these water safety

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: presentations, it really sends that message across.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks what percentage pass the lifeguard qualifying test and whether free prep exists. Williams says the swim improvement program is free and available online; the qualifier is a 50-yard swim in 45 seconds, and 605 participants passed qualifiers last year.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about lifeguard qualifier pass rates and free prep

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And don't forget the nonprofit as well.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What percentage of people who take the lifeguard qualifying test pass it?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And which part do most people fail?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Is there any free prep for people who almost pass it?

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member, for the question.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: So to answer about the prep, our aquatics program does offer what they call the swim improvement program.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: That is free.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: They can find it on the park's website and register for that program to help them get ready to take the qualifier.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: The qualifier itself is a 50-yard swim that they have to pass in 45 seconds.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: That is the qualifier to get into the program.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: Last year, we had 605 participants pass our qualifiers that were offered in all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Narcisse says residents use the Jamaica Bay shoreline even though swimming is not allowed. Focht says Parks posts no-swimming signs and sends Parks Enforcement Patrol officers on weekends and hot days; Narcisse notes her district has no swimming pool.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about Jamaica Bay swimming enforcement and signage

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: My last one.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Residents often use the Jamaica Bay shoreline in my district, even though swimming is not allowed there.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What does parks do about signs, patrols, and outreach in places like that where people swim anyway?

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Any place that we're aware of that has a history of swimming or gathering, we do post signs that say swimming is prohibited.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: They're generally the...

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: have the international symbol of no swimming.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: They're red with white text.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: And then we do have our Parks Enforcement Patrol officers periodically stop by, particularly on a weekend or a hotter day during the summer when they know there may be gatherings there.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: So we approach it both with signage and patrols.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I'm going to leave it with I don't have no swimming pool in my district.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I'm still talking about it.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And my kids cannot swim in the bucket.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So help me out and I'll help you out.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hankerson asks which pools are closed or will close for major repairs. Focht says 51 of 53 outdoor pools were open; Tony D'Apolito is closed but fully funded for a new recreation center with an indoor pool and outdoor aquatic center, and Half End Pool in the Bronx is closed for a $20 million renovation and will reopen next summer.
chapters.title: Hankerson asks which pools are closed for repairs

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Before I go to Councilmember Murano, I do want to acknowledge that we are joined online by Councilmembers Areola and Perina Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Just really quickly, can you provide an update as to which pools are currently closed or will be closed for major repairs and or maintenance or capital work in the near future?

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Of our 53 outdoor pools, 51 were open this year.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: The only two that were closed were Tony D'Apolito, which has been closed for a number of years.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: But the good news there is that we have full funding to do both a new recreation center with an Olympic indoor pool and a new outdoor aquatic center honoring the Keith Haring mural at that site.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: So that's both fully funded.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: And then the other pool that was closed this summer was Half End Pool in the Bronx, which just closed $20-some million renovation.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: It'll open for next summer.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Morano congratulates Parks on the season and asks how many drownings occurred outside lifeguard hours and during the regular season. Focht says Parks does not track drownings outside lifeguard hours; NYPD and the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene do, and Parks will get those numbers.
chapters.title: Morano congratulates Parks and asks about drownings outside lifeguard hours

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Councilmember Marano?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Deputy Commissioner, thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you for the use of props.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I really wish every witness would emulate that.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And congratulations to you and your team.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I think you said you had 16.7 million visitors, the longest beach season in a decade, more than 200 rescues, and most important, no fatalities while lifeguards were on duty in their chairs.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So hats off to you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: It's a tremendous accomplishment, and I don't think we should lose sight of that.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But I do want to follow up on an issue that my colleague, Councilmember Narcisse, raised.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You emphasized that there were zero fatalities or drownings while lifeguards were on duty in their chairs, and I think that's great.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But I think it raises another obvious question, aside from the one my colleague asked.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How many drownings occurred at city beaches?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Outside the hours when lifeguards were on duty.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And of those incidents, how many occurred during the regular swimming season?

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member, for the question.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: And thank you for the props and the props, by the way.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: So we at Parks do not track drownings outside or fatalities outside of the hours that we provide lifeguard security.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: That is tracked through NYPD and the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: There are two city agencies that track those kind of incidences outside of the hours when New York City parks are officially operating our beaches and pools.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: So we would have to get you those numbers, but those are not numbers that rest within parks themselves.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: No, and again, I would appreciate if you could get them to us, understanding that it involves some interagency communication.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Because you can understand if someone drowns at 630 in the evening when a lifeguard went off duty at 6, I'm not sure the family is going to take a great deal of comfort knowing that the Parks Department's official statistics say there were zero fatalities during supervised hours.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I know that's not your fault.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'm not trying to imply that, but I am curious.

chapters.summary: Morano asks what happens if the Council mandates longer hours but Parks lacks qualified lifeguards. Focht says 12-hour days would require nearly double the lifeguards and two full shifts, several hundred more staff, and about $2.5 million per week; without OMB funding it would be an unfunded mandate.
chapters.title: Morano asks what happens if longer hours pass without enough lifeguards

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I appreciated the candor in your testimony about extending the swimming season.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You pointed out that a substantial portion of your workforce consists of teachers and students who simply just won't be available during the proposed extended season.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I think that's actually a pretty compelling practical objection.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But here's what I'd like to know.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If the council passes a law.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: acquiring longer hours, but the department doesn't have enough qualified lifeguards to staff those hours, what actually happens on a practical level?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Do we close portions of the beach?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Do we divert lifeguards from one community to another?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Do we reduce service elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What actually happens if we pass this law and you don't have the staff?

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: I really appreciate the question because I do want to get into this detail about longer hours versus longer season.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: So right now, our beach and pool hours are eight hours for both beaches and pools that our lifeguards can sit in the chairs.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: If we extend the hours and the legislation currently is considering or proposing a 12-hour daily hours,

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: that means we would almost have to double the number of lifeguards we need to hire because we need two full shifts.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: And as you know, again, we've talked a lot about we're getting close to 1,200.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: We need to get to 1,400.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: But 1,400 provides one eight-hour shift at our beaches and pools.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Our lifeguards work six days a week already at both beaches and pools.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: So in order to extend to eight to eight, as the legislation proposes, we would need several hundred more lifeguards.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: And at the moment, I'm not sure where we would get them from.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: We will continue to, again, we're growing about 100 a year, right, for the last four years.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: We got to get to 1,400 before we can even consider going beyond 1,400.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: and expanding those hours.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: To get to the core of your question, what would we do if we don't have enough lifeguards to meet a mandated or legislated obligation?

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: I frankly don't know what we would do because we've never been in that position.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: First of all, we would have to

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: get funding from OMB for both extending the hours and hiring all of those additional lifeguards.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: I would like to note that it costs us about $2.5 million a week to operate our beaches and pools.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: That's our staffing numbers.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: It's about $2.5 million a week.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: For beaches and pools.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: That's largely staff costs for the thousands of lifeguards, maintenance staff, PEP officers.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: And then, of course, there's some money in there for chlorine and toilet paper and trash bags and things like that.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: But both of those things I wanted to offer in response to yours about the challenge of extending the hours and needing a whole other set of lifeguards to run a second shift and the fact that

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: unless we would get funding from OMB, it would be an unfunded mandate at the rate of about $2.5 million a week.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: If I may, Chair.

chapters.summary: Matt Drury notes that the existing administrative code gives the Parks Commissioner discretion on staffing levels, extreme weather, and other conditions. He says if the legislation advances, discussions would likely incorporate those aspects.
chapters.title: Drury notes existing admin code flexibility on staffing and conditions

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Just one procedural note, just in terms of the existing admin code, the commissioner's obviously 100% right.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: There is some flexibility in the current admin code that allows the commissioner, Parks Commissioner, some discretion in terms of taking staffing level requirements, you know, extreme weather, certain conditions.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: So I suspect that, you know, were this legislation to advance, I suspect we'd have discussions about making sure that those sort of aspects were incorporated.

chapters.summary: Morano asks whether a carefully designed pilot program at selected beaches based on demand and staffing would make more sense than a citywide mandate. Focht says it depends on funding and staff, and that expanded hours may be more feasible than an expanded season, but still requires lifeguards, maintenance, and PEP officers.
chapters.title: Morano suggests pilot program for extended hours; Focht cites funding and staffing

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'm wondering, and this is just a question, not a proposal, but would it make more sense to authorize a very carefully designed pilot program at selected beaches based on actual demand and available staffing before imposing a citywide mandate?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You don't like that either.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: No, I can tell you don't like it.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: No, Council Member, I wouldn't say that.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: I would just say, again, it depends on whether or not we would get the funding to do it and could find the staff to do it, both lifeguards, maintenance staff, and PEP officers.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: And, again, I don't know if you're necessarily referring to the expanded hours or the expanded season.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: I think the expanded hours might be a little bit more feasible because it's within the season when we know that people are available to work.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: But I can't emphasize enough that we will simply not be able to hire the people prior to, you know, college students don't become available to the third week in May.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: High school students and teachers don't become available to the very end of June.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: We peak in our employment in the middle of July because by August 1st, we're already losing the college students that are leaving us to have a week or two off before they have to go back to college the third week in August.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: And then, of course, all the public school teachers are leaving us and the high school teachers are leaving us Labor Day weekend to go back to their jobs or school.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: So we will not be able to have the staff to operate beaches and pools outside of the Labor Day to Memorial Day approximate season.

chapters.summary: Morano notes only Rockaway Beach is a true ocean beach and asks whether water safety policies should be tailored by beach. Focht says Parks posts rip current advisories everywhere because visitors may travel between beaches; Morano suggests location-specific risk signage.
chapters.title: Morano asks about tailoring water safety policies by beach

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Two final questions for me.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Your testimony makes an interesting distinction.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You point out among the beaches operated by parks, only Rockaway Beach is technically classified as a true ocean beach.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Its rip current conditions differ from those at the other city beaches, and I think that's an important distinction.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: In my district, we have Wolf's Pond Beach.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Staten Island has its own waterfront conditions and challenges.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Shouldn't the city's water safety policies be tailored to the actual conditions at each beach rather than imposing a one-size-fits-all approach?

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: I would say possibly.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: I think our approach at Parks has always been, as I mentioned, posting the rip current advisories in all of the restrooms.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: In other words, we took the maximum worst condition or the maximum saturation of messaging and put it everywhere.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Because truthfully, somebody could enjoy a day at Wolf's Pond and then travel to Rockaways, and they should know about the rip currents at Rockaways, even though they're not going to encounter them at South or Midland or Cedar or Wolf.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I mean, it would seem to me that location-specific risk signage might be more prudent.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And finally— Counselor, if you can ask your final question.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: That's why I was here at 1 o'clock, to get all these in for the multiple rounds.

chapters.summary: Morano asks whether Parks has calculated the five- or ten-year cost of digital signage. Focht says no estimate yet because the bill was introduced last week and long-term costs are speculative; Drury says OMB may have a fiscal impact statement, but over 200 beach entrances may lack utilities and costs are considerable.
chapters.title: Morano asks if Parks estimated digital signage costs

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You described digital signage at beaches as exceptionally difficult and expensive to maintain because of sand, salt, spray, wind, and vandalism.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: That sounds reasonable.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But here's what troubles me.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Have you actually calculated what it would cost to install, operate, maintain, and replace these signs over five or ten years?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And have you provided that estimate to the council?

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: We have not because the most recent introduction was just made last week, so we've not had the time to talk to manufacturers and see what that cost might be.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: And certainly the long-term five- or ten-year operational cost would be somewhat speculation because we have nothing like this.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: If I can, sorry, just quickly on a process note, we are in communication with OMB, who I believe is compiling and may have already submitted a fiscal impact statement.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: For this bill specifically, it presents a really unique challenge because of the factors that were mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: And there are significant unknowns about the over 200 beach entrances, which may lack electricity, utility connections, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: Would be a challenge to get a highly detailed, but we have certainly, you know, working with OMB to kind of provide some sense of that.

utterances.speaker: Matt Drury
utterances.text: But on its face, considerable, very, very considerable.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Thanks very much.

chapters.summary: Narcisse follows up on darkness in October and the proposed 8 p.m. closing. Focht says lifeguards must be able to see swimmers; dusk in late September and October is around 6:15 to 6:40, so keeping beaches open until 8 p.m. until October 15 would be unsafe regardless of staffing.
chapters.title: Narcisse follows up on dusk and 8 p.m. beach closing

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I know Councilmember Narsi's had a follow-up.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I'm going to extend Councilmember Santos-Wosso's time.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: You can give your follow-up.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: The thing that I want you to clarify for me is about the dust we talk about, which I know in October is starting to get dark.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So if you can kind of highlight this for me, it can be clear in my mind.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Again, the paramount need to ensure public safety for swimmers is for the lifeguards to be able to see the swimmers in the water, and particularly at beaches when they may be looking quite a distance out.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: So you simply need to look at any chart, and you'll see when dusk is.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: And again, in October, late September, October,

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Dusk is anywhere from 6.15 to 6.30, 6.40, approximately that time.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: And then obviously it gets earlier and earlier and earlier as we get into October.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: So, again, the legislation would propose keeping the beaches open until 8 p.m.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Until October 15th.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Setting aside whether or not we would have the lifeguards, it simply would not be safe because they could not see the swimmers in the water.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

chapters.summary: Santosuosso, representing Coney Island, asks about barriers to reaching 1,400 lifeguards. Focht says there are few major hurdles and the main issue is awareness; Williams says Parks has not worked closely with NYCHA but will reach out, and Santosuosso offers to help recruit in nearby NYCHA developments.
chapters.title: Santosuosso asks about recruitment barriers and NYCHA outreach

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Council President Swanson.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, and thank you so much for being here.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I am the proud representative of Coney Island, and so many of my questions today pertain to our beaches in my district.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: But first of all, I want to echo Councilmember Morano's congratulations on the progress that we're making in terms of lifeguard recruitment and retention.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I know it's not easy.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I guess first I'd like to just start by saying what do you see as the main barriers to recruitment and retention to getting to that 1,400 number right now?

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you, Council Member, and good to see you.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: At this point, I would say there are not many major hurdles as we've encountered in the last several years.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Again, I think we've addressed many of them with the increased salary, the retention bonus, the really aggressive marketing campaign, all of the partnerships, expanding to all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: It's really just awareness, and this is where you and your colleagues and all of our partners sitting in the audience can help us advertise.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Again, we opened the portal this Sunday for people.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: to register and we start qualifiers December 1st.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: So please, please, if you're interested in being a New York City lifeguard, sign up through the portal starting Sunday, get your qualifying time, get your sort of qualifying appointment,

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: and come out and swim for us.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: So, and I'm glad you mentioned that because I believe in your testimony, you mentioned partnerships with city agencies in order to get the word out.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Can you detail any efforts in NYCHA?

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner Folk.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: We haven't worked closely with NYCHA, Councilmember, but that is something that we will.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: We do send them a digital mailing, and we do send them a snail mail, but we will reach out to them to see if there's something more extensively we can do.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Let me sign myself up to help.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And, you know, the west end of Coney Island, of course, abuts something like nine or ten NYCHA developments.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And I think it would be really advantageous to do some targeted recruitment in those developments because, as you said, you're doing an effort to sort of recruit lifeguards and place them near where they live.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: These are folks who live within walking distance to the beach, and I think it would be a really beautiful thing if we did some heightened recruitment within those NYCHA buildings in order to bring people out to lifeguard where they live.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Yeah, okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: We'll do that together.

chapters.summary: Santosuosso says there was a mid-season gap in lifeguard coverage on the West End of Coney Island. She asks for a permanent plan to ensure equitable staffing so residents do not feel that part of the beach is less valued.
chapters.title: Santosuosso seeks permanent lifeguard coverage for Coney Island West End

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And I want to also just thank you for your efforts this past summer.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: About midway through the season, we realized that there was a real gap in lifeguard coverage on the West End, which I think

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: is probably not an intentional thing, but does send the message to West End residents that that part of the beach is not as valued or prioritized as further east towards Brighton.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And kind of every year we do a little bit of catch up to make sure that those are staffed.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And I just want to say, you know, going into this season, I would love a permanent plan to just make sure there's equity there so that there is regular lifeguard staff.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: in the West End.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: This is one of those cases where we think of Coney Island and we don't think of West End or further towards the amusement districts, but the folks that live near the West End, they are going to go swimming there where there's no lifeguards.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And I think it would send a really strong message from the city if we would make sure, you know, that there was consistent lifeguard coverage there without us sort of scrambling mid-season.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: But I will help you in hoping to do some of that recruitment with NYCHA.

chapters.summary: Santosuosso asks about public school recruitment efforts, especially for Coney Island. Williams details banners at every high school, digital marketing through schools, PSAL partnerships, attendance at swim meets, and qualifiers and training at public high schools.
chapters.title: Santosuosso asks about public school lifeguard recruitment

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And then I'm sorry if you said this while I was gone, but I would love to just hear a little bit more, again, I'm thinking Coney Island, of your efforts to recruit in partnership with public schools.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: Councilmember, thank you, and I look forward to speaking with you about reaching out to NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: We work extensively with New York City Public Schools.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: Again, we sit on the Lifeguard and Safety Task Force that they sit on, as well as a lot of the nonprofits that are here and not with us today, the YMCAs.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: We have banners that go up at every high school.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: We have a digital marketing campaign that goes out through their social media.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: Our social media is emailed to parents and students.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: We work with PSAL.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: We attend all the swim meets to recruit.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: Our lifeguards go out and explain what an amazing job this is.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: And, you know, we just work very closely with them.

utterances.speaker: Bonnie Williams
utterances.text: We do qualifiers at the high schools and the other schools, and we also do training at public high schools.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Awesome.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thank you for all of your efforts, and I look forward to working together.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hankerson asks whether parks workers clear public assets outside parks during snowstorms. Focht says Parks commits vehicles and drivers to DSNY for 12-hour shifts to clear residential streets, and Parks staff clear bus stops, hydrants, and crosswalks on sidewalks adjacent to parks property.
chapters.title: Hankerson questions Focht on parks workers clearing snow outside parks

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you have any further questions?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Okay, before we move to public testimony, I do have a couple of questions that are unrelated to the current topic.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: So if you can just indulge me for just three minutes, especially as we prepare for the snow season.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Are there times when parks workers are assigned to clear public assets outside of parks?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: During snowstorms?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member, for the question.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: When you say, I'm just pausing because when you say public and I'm switching my mind from swimming in beaches to snow.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: No worries.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: So we have a longstanding commitment where during certain intense winter storms, we do commit.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: A certain number of vehicles and drivers to DSNY, they're deployed to DSNY, on 12-hour shifts to help clear residential streets.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: So it is a public asset, the residential street, but it's not a park asset.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: So that would be the only instance that I can think of where parks employees are employed in winter weather response, not on parks property.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: In those instances, who gives them directives?

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: DSNY does.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: DSNY gives them routes.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Are they oftentimes assigned to do the same work as the emergency snow shovelers?

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: That's clearing bus stops, hydrants, sidewalks.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: No, this is vehicles.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: So this is pickup trucks with plows on.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: This is pickup trucks with plows on plowing smaller scale residential streets.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I just wanted to get that on the record.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: You're sure about that.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: No city parks workers are assigned to shuffle outside of parks property areas that include bus stops, fire hydrants, sidewalks.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: So our park staff.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Clear bus stops, fire hydrants, and crosswalks on sidewalks adjacent to parks property because they're ours.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: So if you have Central Park and you have Fifth Avenue and you have a bus stop on Fifth Avenue, that bus stop will be cleared by park staff.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: So we are clearing crosswalks, fire hydrants, and bus stops on perimeter sidewalks around all parks property.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Nothing else?

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Nowhere else, rather.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Nowhere else.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Mark Focht
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Thank you for testifying today.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I hope that you can stick around for the public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: If you can, please do, because I think it shouldn't just be the committee hearing, but also the agency hearing from the advocates.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I now open this hearing for public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: I remind members of the public that this is a formal government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony and may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant at Arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant at Arms and wait to be recognized.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: When recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on today's hearing topic, the state of water safety at the city's beaches and pools, and intros 262, 957, 1163, and 1164.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: With that, the first...

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: If you have written testimony, if you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant at Arms.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: You may also email written testimony to testimony at council.nyc.gov or any other council email address within 72 hours of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Ty Hankerson
utterances.text: Audio and video recordings will not be accepted.

utterances.text: All right.

utterances.text: It's for, thank you.
